messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 48

# Vignette: Kareem

Kareem is a 56-year-old Lebanese-American man who has been married to his wife, Nadia, for nearly thirty years. He works as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit, a job he took up later in life after years in retail management. He is a careful, observant man — someone who, by his own description, has always paid close attention to the world around him. That attentiveness, once a quiet strength, has become something he can no longer turn off.

Three years ago, Kareem was driving home from a late evening at the office when he was pulled over for a broken tail light he hadn't known about. What followed was not a routine stop. Within minutes, he was ordered out of the car at gunpoint, forced to the ground, and held face-down on the asphalt with an officer's knee pressed into his back while a second officer shouted at him not to move. He remembers the texture of the pavement against his cheek, the smell of exhaust, the cold. He was detained for nearly forty minutes before being released without charges or explanation. No one apologized. He drove the rest of the way home in silence and did not tell Nadia what had happened until the following morning.

In the weeks after, Kareem told himself he was fine. He went to work. He posted content, managed comment threads, monitored engagement metrics. But he began to notice that he was scanning every piece of content differently — images of police, flashing lights, any video involving a confrontation would stop him cold. His hands would go still over the keyboard. He would find himself back on that street, cheek against the pavement, certain he was about to die. He started muting keywords, building filters, restructuring his workflow so that a junior colleague handled anything flagged as sensitive. He told her it was a delegation decision. It was not.

At home, Kareem sleeps poorly. He wakes between two and four in the morning and lies rigid in the dark, listening. He has begun checking the locks multiple times before bed, and he parks his car differently now — always facing out, always near a light. Nadia has noticed. She reaches for him in the night and sometimes he flinches before he can stop himself. He hates that. He hates what it communicates without his permission.

He rarely drives after dark anymore. When he must, he grips the wheel with both hands and watches the rearview mirror more than the road ahead. Twice he has taken alternate routes home to avoid passing a police substation on his usual street. He does not think of this as avoidance. He thinks of it as being sensible.

What troubles Kareem most is the anger, which arrives without warning and with a force that frightens him. He grew up in Beirut during the civil war and survived things he does not speak about easily. He thought he understood violence, thought he had made a kind of peace with the world's capacity for it. But this particular incident — being pressed into American asphalt by American hands, in the city where he has lived for twenty-five years and raised two daughters — broke something open that he does not have words for yet. He feels it as a deep and persistent shame, though he knows, intellectually, that the shame belongs to someone else.

He describes himself to his wife as tired. She knows it is more than that. He knows it is more than that. He sits at his desk each morning, opens his laptop, and begins the careful work of managing how the world sees things — curating image, shaping narrative, deciding what to show and what to suppress. He is very good at it. And he is aware, with a kind of hollow irony, that he has become equally skilled at performing the same function on himself.
